title: Meridian Air: the Northport route
prompt: Our client is Meridian Air, a mid-sized regional carrier. It has two aircraft coming off lease commitments next year and is deciding whether to deploy them on a new route between Castleton and Northport — a corridor it does not fly today, and where three carriers already compete. The CEO wants to know whether to launch.

questions.prompt: Before you frame the problem, what should you check with the client? Select the two most relevant.
options: What return does Meridian need on these two aircraft, and by when?
How large is the Castleton–Northport market, and how is it shared today?
What is the average age of Meridian's fleet?
How many cabin crew are based in Castleton?
What is Meridian's current on-time performance?

optionRationale: Without a hurdle you cannot say whether a profitable route is a good route. The aircraft have alternative uses.
Entry cases live or die on the size of the pool and how hard the incumbents will fight for it.
Fleet age affects maintenance cost, which is already inside the cost-per-flight assumption.
A staffing detail, and one that follows the launch decision rather than informing it.
A service metric that says nothing about whether this route earns its aircraft.
commonMistakes: Treating a positive operating profit as a yes without asking what the aircraft could earn elsewhere
Framing the route in isolation from the competitors already flying it

questions.followUp:
On the objective: the board will only release the two aircraft to this route if it clears $5M of annual operating profit by year three. Below that, the aircraft go to an existing route instead.

On the market: the corridor carries 3,000,000 passengers a year, shared between three carriers. Here is the picture, along with the plan the client's network team has built.

questions.prompt: How would you decide whether Meridian should launch this route? Select the four areas you would investigate.
options: Standalone route economics: revenue, variable cost per flight, and route fixed costs
The share Meridian would have to win, and where it would have to come from
How the three incumbents would respond, and how much room each has to respond on price
The opportunity cost of the two aircraft against their next best deployment
Meridian's loyalty programme redemption rates
The historic profitability of Meridian's oldest route
The airport's terminal refurbishment schedule

optionRationale: The base case. Everything else is a stress test on this.
An entry plan is a share plan: 378,000 passengers have to come from somewhere.
The reason entry cases fail. A plan that only works if nobody reacts is not a plan.
The board framed the decision this way, so the comparison has to be against the alternative use.
A retention detail on routes Meridian already flies.
Historic and unrelated to this corridor's economics.
Operationally relevant one day, decision-irrelevant today.
commonMistakes: Building a standalone P&L and stopping there, with no competitive response and no opportunity cost
Treating market attractiveness as a substitute for Meridian's own economics

questions.followUp: Good — and note the order. Size the base case first, then ask how much of it survives a competitive response. Let's build the base case.

questions.prompt: Using the operating plan, how many passengers would the route carry in its first full year?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in thousands of passengers — for 250,000 passengers, type 250.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
4 round trips a day is 8 flights a day.
Seats offered: 8 × 180 × 350 = 504,000 a year.
At a 75% load factor: 504,000 × 0.75 = 378,000 passengers.
commonMistakes: Treating 4 round trips as 4 flights and halving the answer
Applying the load factor to flights rather than to seats
Using 365 days when the plan says 350 operating days

questions.followUp: 378,000 passengers, from 504,000 seats offered. Hold on to both numbers — the gap between them is where the risk sits.

questions.prompt: What annual operating profit would the route generate in its first full year?

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Revenue: 378,000 passengers × $100 = $37.8M.
Variable cost: 8 flights × 350 days = 2,800 flights × $12,000 = $33.6M.
Fixed cost: $3.0M.
Operating profit: $37.8M − $33.6M − $3.0M = $1.2M.
commonMistakes: Costing per round trip rather than per flight, halving the variable cost
Forgetting the $3M of route fixed costs
Multiplying the fare by seats rather than by passengers

questions.followUp:
$1.2M — against a hurdle of $5M. On the client's own assumptions the route falls $3.8M short of the number the board set.

Before we conclude anything, let's test how robust that $1.2M is.

questions.prompt: What share of the Castleton–Northport market does the plan implicitly assume Meridian wins in its first year?

commonMistakes: Dividing by seats offered rather than by the market size
Assuming the market grows to absorb Meridian, when nothing in the data says it does

questions.followUp: 12.6% — roughly one passenger in eight, in year one, taken from three established carriers. Nothing in the plan says where those passengers come from.

questions.prompt: Look at the competitive picture alongside the plan. Select the three statements the exhibits support.
options: At $100, Meridian would price about 15% below the market's average fare but about 18% above ValueJet
The plan requires taking roughly one passenger in eight from three established carriers in year one
ValueJet has the most room to respond on price, since it already carries the lowest fare and 600,000 passengers
Skylink's 45% share makes it the carrier least likely to defend the route
The market's average fare of $118 shows the plan's $100 fare is conservative

optionRationale: True: the share-weighted average fare is $118, so $100 is 15% below it — but 18% above ValueJet's $85.
True: 12.6% of the market, with no stated source of those passengers.
True, and it is the sharpest threat: the low-fare incumbent is the one Meridian's positioning attacks.
False, and backwards: the largest incumbent has the most passengers to lose and the deepest pockets to defend them.
False: at $100 the route already needs a 72.6% load factor to break even. That is not conservatism.
commonMistakes: Reading '$100 is below the average' as 'Meridian is the cheap option' — ValueJet is $15 cheaper
Assuming a large incumbent is a complacent one

questions.followUp:
So Meridian would enter as the second-cheapest carrier, not the cheapest, needing one passenger in eight, against an incumbent that can undercut it and a market leader with the most to lose.

Now let's put a number on how much room the plan actually has.

questions.prompt: At the planned $100 fare, what load factor does the route need simply to break even?

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Total cost: $33.6M variable + $3.0M fixed = $36.6M.
Passengers needed at $100: $36.6M / $100 = 366,000.
Seats offered: 504,000.
Break-even load factor: 366,000 / 504,000 = 72.6%.
commonMistakes: Leaving the $3M of fixed costs out and answering 66.7%
Dividing by planned passengers instead of by seats offered
Treating the cost per flight as a cost per passenger

questions.followUp:
72.6%, against a plan of 75%. The whole business case sits in 2.4 points of load factor — about 12,000 passengers a year, or roughly 34 a day across eight flights.

That is the fragility. Now let's price it.

questions.prompt: Suppose ValueJet responds and Meridian has to hold its fare at $90 rather than $100, while still carrying the planned 378,000 passengers. What is the route's operating result?
questions.answerFormatNote: This is a loss. Enter its size in $ millions, without a minus sign.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Revenue at $90: 378,000 × $90 = $34.02M.
Total cost is unchanged at $36.6M.
Result: $34.02M − $36.6M = −$2.58M, a loss of $2.58M.
commonMistakes: Reducing costs alongside the fare; the cost per flight does not move with the fare
Applying the 10% fare cut to the $1.2M profit rather than to the revenue line
Assuming a lower fare fills more seats, which the question explicitly rules out

questions.followUp:
A $10 fare cut — 10% — turns a $1.2M profit into a $2.58M loss, because every dollar of fare falls straight through to the bottom line while the cost base does not move.

That is the shape of the decision: a route that misses its hurdle at plan, and loses money on any realistic competitive response.

questions.prompt: If Meridian launches anyway, what should it do to protect the economics of the route? Select the three strongest moves.
options: Launch at reduced frequency and build up, so fixed costs and exposure scale with demonstrated demand
Target segments the incumbents serve badly — off-peak times, connecting traffic, corporate contracts — rather than competing head-on on price
Secure the cost base: negotiate airport charges and handling contracts before launch, so the break-even load factor falls
Match ValueJet's $85 fare from day one to buy share quickly
Commit both aircraft immediately to signal permanence to the incumbents
Delay the decision until the next fare cycle and re-run the analysis

optionRationale: Directly attacks the fragility: less fixed cost committed before the demand is proven.
The only way to win 12.6% without triggering the price war that the $90 case shows Meridian loses.
Every dollar off the cost base lowers the 72.6% break-even, which is the binding constraint.
At $85 the route loses roughly $4.5M a year — it buys share by destroying the economics.
Maximises committed cost against the least proven demand, which is the opposite of what the numbers say.
Not a protective move at all; it defers the decision without changing anything.
commonMistakes: Reaching for price as the entry weapon when the sensitivity shows price is where Meridian is weakest
Confusing commitment with strategy on a route with 2.4 points of headroom

questions.followUp: All three do the same thing in different ways: they lower the break-even, or they win passengers somewhere other than on headline fare. Neither of those is in the client's current plan.

questions.prompt: The CEO has two minutes before a board call. Give your recommendation in seven to eight lines maximum.

keyPoints: Leads with the recommendation: do not launch on the current plan
Gives the headline number — $1.2M against a $5M hurdle, a $3.8M shortfall
Names the fragility: a 72.6% break-even against a 75% plan, so 2.4 points of load factor carry the whole case
Shows the sensitivity: a $10 fare cut produces a $2.58M loss, and the plan needs 12.6% share from three incumbents
Names the opportunity cost of the two aircraft explicitly
Offers the conditional path: relaunch the case at lower frequency, with a secured cost base and a segment-led plan rather than a price-led one
Stays inside eight lines and does not narrate the calculation
commonMistakes: Recommending launch because the route is profitable, when profitable is not the test the board set
Giving a flat no with no conditions under which the answer would change
Burying the hurdle comparison beneath the arithmetic

closing: That is the end of the case. Your transcript is ready — copy it into an LLM to be graded on what you actually said, not on what you meant.
